items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to requiring Medicaid coverage of both blood testing and skin prick testing for allergies
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S1222

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the social services law, in relation
to requiring Medicaid coverage of both blood testing and skin prick
testing for allergies

 PURPOSE: :

To ensure that the Medicaid program provides access to blood allergy
testing in parity with skin prick testing, as the tests are clinically
equivalent, cost equivalent, and would expand access to testing, which
would be an important step in addressing health disparities.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS: :

Section 1 creates a new section of the Social Services Law entitled
"blood allergy testing," which would require the department to treat
serologic-specific IgE allergy tests (blood allergy tests) and
percutaneous skin allergy tests (skin prick tests) as equivalent in
their sensitivity and accuracy for confirming the existence of an
allergy in a patient, and to treat those tests as medically necessary
for those individuals with a medical history consistent with specified
conditions. The bill would require the department to update its
provider bulletins, as necessary, to reference the most current
professional literature and guidance related to allergy testing.

Section 2 is the effective date of the bill.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Historically, allergies were diagnosed by an allergist who used a
percutaneous, or "skin-prick," test to infect the skin of a patient
with varying allergens for the purpose of determining the patient's
reaction to those allergens. This procedure required the patient to be
referred by his or her primary care physician to an allergist, and
required the patient to undergo a series of pricks to his or her skin.

Advances in blood testing technology using serologic-specific IgE
quantitative testing allow a patient to be diagnosed without a
referral to a specialist. Professional literature and guidance from
the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute at the National
Institutes of Health has determined that blood tests and skin tests
for allergies are equal in their diagnostic value, and that blood
testing is preferred in the case of testing for food allergies.
Medicaid coverage decisions must be based on the latest and most
current medical literature and studies.

Private health care insurance plans recognize the professional
literature and guidelines regarding the efficacy of blood testing and
cover blood testing for the diagnosis of allergies. New York State
Medicaid does not cover blood testing for allergies at all; only skin
prick testing is covered. Due to an insufficient number of allergists
available to diagnose and treat Medicaid patients, the diagnosis of
many patients covered by Medicaid is delayed or never occurs.
Creating access to this blood test would help improve population
health and address health care disparities, particularly in
underserved communities.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY: :

2016: S7450

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS: :



Because blood allergy testing is cost-equivalent to skin prick
testing, it is not anticipated that this bill will have a significant
fiscal impact.

 EFFECTIVE DATE: :

This act shall take effect the first of July next succeeding the date
upon which it shall become law, effective immediately, the
commissioner of health shall promulgate all rules and regulations
deemed necessary and desirable to implement the provisions of this act
on or before its effective date.

VETO MESSAGE - No. 183
 
TO THE SENATE:
 
I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:
 
Senate Bill Number 1222, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT  to amend the social services law, in relation to requiring
      Medicaid coverage of both blood testing and skin prick testing for
      allergies"
 
    NOT APPROVED
 
  The bill would add a new section to the Social Services Law to require
the State Medicaid program to treat blood serologic-specific  IgE  tests
(blood  allergy  tests)  and percutaneous skin allergy tests (skin prick
tests) as equivalent confirmatory tests in terms  of  their  sensitivity
and accuracy. The bill would also require Medicaid to treat blood aller-
gy  tests  as  medically  necessary  for  individuals  with a history of
certain types of conditions such as inhalant or food allergies. I  fully
support  the  intent  of  this bill of ensuring that Medicaid recipients
have access to the allergy testing they  require  to  properly  diagnose
specific  allergens.  However,  as  drafted, the bill raises a number of
concerns and ultimately does not accomplish this goal.
 
  First, Medicaid already treats blood  allergy  tests  and  skin  prick
tests  as  equivalent confirmatory tests. Second, on June 1, 2016, Medi-
caid expanded medically necessary coverage for blood allergy testing  to
include  patients with skin conditions, children under the age of three,
and individuals unable to discontinue  medications  such  as  antihista-
mines.  Third,  by  encouraging the use of blood allergy tests, the bill
would have the unintended consequence of reducing the number of patients
obtaining accurate diagnoses by allergy  specialists.  Since  both  skin
prick  and  blood  allergy tests have a low level of accuracy, a primary
care provider may not have the experience nor expertise to make accurate
diagnoses or manage an allergy diagnosis, including developing an appro-
priate treatment plan. It is therefore very important for patients  with
suspected allergies to be seen and tested by an allergist who can deter-
mine with more precision the specific allergens that should be evaluated
for  each  patient given their health history, and develop and monitor a
plan or care, which may include allergen injections or allergen exposure
treatments. Finally, as this bill would generate an increase  in  refer-
rals for blood allergy tests by primary care physicians, it would result
in a significant, unbudgeted fiscal impact on the Medicaid program. At a
time  when  the Federal government has enacted, and is threatening addi-
tional, devastating cuts to the State's health care system, it would  be
irresponsible  to  incur  such  unbudgeted costs at this time. For these
reasons I am forced to veto this bill.
 
  The bill is disapproved.                    (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO
 
                               __________
